'''''Pyrrhopappus pauciflorus''''', commonly known as '''smallflower desert-chicory''', '''Texas false dandelion''' or '''Texas dandelion''', is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Asteraceae]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.tropicos.org/Name/50141494|title=Tropicos {{!}} Name - Pyrrhopappus pauciflorus (D. Don) DC.|website=www.tropicos.org|access-date=2020-01-06}}</ref> It is native to the [[southern United States]] and [[northern Mexico]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=406950|title=Taxonomy - GRIN-Global Web v 1.10.5.0|website=npgsweb.ars-grin.gov|access-date=2020-01-06}}</ref> It is a weedy annual found in prairies, clay soils and disturbed habitats such as fields and sidewalks.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250067416|title=Pyrrhopappus pauciflorus in Flora of North America @ efloras.org|website=efloras.org|access-date=2020-01-06}}</ref>

== Description ==
The Texas dandelion is a [[taproot]] that grows 6 to 20 inches (15 to 50 centimeters) in height.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=False dandelion (Plants of the Middle Rio Grande Bosque) · iNaturalist |url=https://www.inaturalist.org/guide_taxa/1144669 |access-date=2024-04-03 |website=iNaturalist |language=en}}</ref> Its petals open in the morning and stay open through midday,<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2019-10-22 |title=Texas Dandelion |url=https://www.gardenstylesanantonio.com/garden-tips-blog/plant/texas-dandelion/ |access-date=2024-04-03 |website=Garden Style San Antonio |language=en-US}}</ref> and the plant typically blooms from March to May. When broken, the stem produces a milky sap. Seeds dry out to resemble [[Taraxacum|dandelion]] puffs.<ref name=":0" />

According to the [[United States Geological Survey|U.S. Geological Survey]], "The upper leaves of ''Pyrrhopappus pauciflorus'' are [[Pinnation|pinnatifid]] with usually 2 or 3 linear lobes on each side and lower leaves that are usually pinnatifid, sometimes merely toothed late in the season. [It has] hairless, clasping, cauline leaves."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Plants of Louisiana |url=https://warcapps.usgs.gov/PlantID/Species/Details/2172#:~:text=The%20upper%20leaves%20of%20Pyrrhopappus%20pauciflorus |access-date=2024-04-03 |website=warcapps.usgs.gov}}</ref>

''P. pauciflorus'' is similar in appearance to ''[[Pyrrhopappus carolinianus|P. carolinianus]]'' but has [[trichome]]s on its stems, which the latter lacks.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Plants of Louisiana |url=https://warcapps.usgs.gov/PlantID/Species/Details/2173 |access-date=2024-04-03 |website=warcapps.usgs.gov}}</ref>

== Etymology and history ==
The scientific name ''Pyrrhopappus pauciflorus'' has many roots, with "pyrrhos" meaning fiery or red-colored, "[[Pappus (botany)|pappus]]" referring to the unique sepals of Asteraceae.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Asteraceae - Daisy, Sunflower, Composite {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/plant/Asteraceae/Flowers |access-date=2024-04-03 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en}}</ref>

Scottish botanist [[David Don]] (1799–1841) first named the species, calling it ''Chondrilla pauciflora'' in his 1830 article "Descriptions of the new Genera and Species of the Class Compositœ belonging to the Floras of Peru, Mexico, and Chile."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Don |first=David |date=1830 |title=Descriptions of the new Genera and Species of the Class Compositœ belonging to the Floras of Peru, Mexico, and Chile |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/part/25012 |journal=Transactions of the Linnean Society of London |volume=16 |pages=169––297 |doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.1829.tb00136.x}}</ref>

The flower was described as ''Pyrrhopappus pauciflorus'' by [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle]] (1778–1841) in volume 7 of his 17-volume series on plant classification'', [[Prodromus Systematis Naturalis Regni Vegetabilis|Prodromus systematis naturalis regni vegetabilis]].''<ref>{{Cite book |last=de Candolle |first=Augustin Pyramus |title=Prodromus systematis naturalis regni vegetabilis, sive, Enumeratio contracta ordinum generum specierumque plantarum huc usque cognitarium, juxta methodi naturalis, normas digesta |date=1838 |pages=143–144 |language=Latin |trans-title=Prodrome of the natural system of the vegetable kingdom, or, A contracted enumeration of the orders of the genera and species of plants hitherto known, according to the natural method, arranged according to the rules}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
[[File:Pyrrhopappus pauciflorus seeds.jpg|left|thumb|266x266px|Pyrrhopappus pauciflorus in the seed-bearing stage in College Station, Texas.]]
Texas dandelion serves as a food source for several local species; [[cattle]] and [[white-tailed deer]] eat the leaves and stems, and [[Turkey (bird)|Rio Grande turkeys]] eat the seeds.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Everitt |first=J.H. |title=Field guide to the broad leaved herbaceous plants of South Texas used by livestock and wildlife |date=1999 |publisher=Texas Tech University Press |location=Lubbock |pages=59}}</ref> It attracts small pollinators, similar to related flowers.<ref name=":1" />

== Cultivation and uses ==
As a freeze-hardy native wildflower, Texas dandelion can grow in full or partial sun and requires little water. It prefers well-drained soil, such as sand or clay. It can grow under tree canopies as well as in grasslands.<ref name=":1" />

Roots can be used to brew [[Dandelion coffee|dandelion tea or coffee]]. The leaves are edible but have a bitter taste, so they're often boiled before eating. It's also possible to make [[Fruit preserves|jelly]] out of Texas dandelion. According to physical organic chemist and forager [https://medicinemanplantco.com/pages/dr-mark-merriwether-vorderbruggen Mark "Merriwether" Vorderbruggen], "The bitter flavor of the roots are becoming popular with high-end bartenders making their own concoctions where these roots replace traditional bitters."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ph.D |first=Mark Merriwether Vorderbruggen |title=Texas Dandelion |url=https://www.foragingtexas.com/2011/10/texas-dandelion.html |access-date=2024-04-03 |language=en}}</ref>
